Oui, **c’est le principe**, avec une distinction importante : **Bearer** désigne la façon de transmettre le jeton ; **JWT** désigne un format possible du jeton.

### Connexion Azure par navigateur

Le parcours repose généralement sur **OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect avec Microsoft Entra ID** :

```text
Extension VS Code
  → ouvre la page de connexion Microsoft
  → l’utilisateur s’authentifie, éventuellement avec MFA
  → le flux renvoie un code d’autorisation
  → le client obtient un jeton d’accès
  → appels API avec Authorization: Bearer <jeton>
```

Un autre flux possible est le **device code** : VS Code fournit un code à saisir dans le navigateur, puis obtient le jeton après validation.

L’extension **ne récupère pas ton mot de passe**. Elle reçoit une session ou un jeton via le mécanisme d’authentification. Le jeton d’accès est limité par une audience, des permissions et une expiration ; son renouvellement peut être géré par le fournisseur d’authentification. Un **ID token** identifie l’utilisateur, mais ne remplace pas le jeton d’accès destiné à l’API.

### Pour notre extension Scaleway

Actuellement, nous utilisons une **clé API**, transmise :
- en `X-Auth-Token` pour les API de contrôle ;
- en `Authorization: Bearer` pour l’API serverless.

**Mettre une clé dans un header Bearer ne la transforme pas en JWT ni en connexion OAuth.**

Pour proposer la même expérience navigateur qu’Azure, il faut vérifier que Scaleway expose un **flux OAuth utilisable par une extension tierce**, avec inscription du client, permissions et mécanisme de retour adaptés. La connexion web de la console Scaleway ne suffit pas à établir cette possibilité.

**La bonne prochaine vérification est donc le support officiel d’une authentification déléguée Scaleway**, avant de développer une fenêtre de login. On ne doit ni collecter le mot de passe Scaleway dans notre extension, ni récupérer les cookies ou jetons internes de la console.

title: Set up identity federation
description: This page shows you how to set up identity federation on your Organization
dates:

import Requirements from '@macros/iam/requirements.mdx'

Scaleway supports Identity Federation to provide your teams with secure access to their accounts via Single Sign-On (SSO). Depending on your organization’s requirements, you can use either built-in OAuth2 providers or configure SAML for centralized identity management.


| Feature | **OAuth2** | **SAML** |
|--------|-------------------------------|--------|
| **Availability** | Enabled by default for all organizations | Available, but requires setup |
| **Supported Providers** | Google, GitHub | Any SAML-compatible Identity Provider |
| **Setup Required** | No | Yes — must be configured by an IAM admin |
| **User Access** | Any Scaleway member whose email is verified with Google or GitHub | Only users explicitly defined in the Identity Provider |
| **Centralized Management** | No | Yes — manage users from your Identity Provider |

<Message type="important">
  Keep in mind that:
  - Each authentication method (SAML SSO, OAuth2 SSO, authentication code, password) can be enabled or disabled inside the Organization. Members can only authenticate using methods that an IAM admin has enabled.
  - SSO with SAML does not apply to an Organization's Owner. Owners can log in with SSO with OAuth2.
</Message>

Follow the steps below to set up Identity Federation for your Organization through SAML at Scaleway.

<Requirements />

- A Scaleway account logged into the [console](https://console.scaleway.com)
- [Owner](/iam/concepts/glossary/#owner) status or [IAM permissions](/iam/concepts/glossary/#permission) allowing you to perform actions in the intended Organization
- An Identity Provider (IdP) configured in your company, making sure it includes all users who need to access Scaleway. Some examples of IdPs:
   - Okta
   - OneLogin
   - Microsoft Entra ID (prev. Azure AD)
   - PingIdentity
   - Google Workspace
   - Authentik

## Set up a SAML connection

1. Go to your security settings.
2. Scroll to the **Configure Identity Federation** section.
3. Click **Set up SAML SSO**. A pop-up appears.
4. Copy the URLs displayed in the pop-up.

    The information in the first step are the URLs referring to Scaleway that will be requested by your Identity Provider to create a link between platforms. They are:
        - The assertion consumer service (ACS) URL, and
        - Scaleway's entity ID

5. Click **Import identity provider data**.
6. Upload your identity provider metadata. Most identity providers supply an XML file export of your configuration. You can upload this file to automatically set up SAML.
    <Message type="important">
    Alternatively, you can click **Set up manually** to manually enter the IdP's metadata. This is the information referring to your Identity Provider that Scaleway needs to confirm the connection. It can be found in your IdP's configuration page. The metadata includes:
        - **Single Sign-On URL** - This is the URL your members will be redirected to when logging in with SAML
        - **The Identity Provider's Entity ID**
    </Message>
7. Click **Submit**.
8. Enter the signing certificate generated by your Identity Provider in the box.
    <Message type="important">
    Keep in mind that:
    - Only base64-encoded certificates are supported.
    - The certificate must have an expiration date.
    - Your certificate entry must start with:
        ```
        -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
        ```
        And end with:
        ```
        -----END CERTIFICATE-----
        ```
    </Message>

    <Message type="note">
      You can close the Identity Provider pop-up without adding the certificate right away. The certificate can [be added at a later time](#how-to-add-a-certificate). However, while the certificate is not added, the connection between Scaleway and your Identity Provider will not be complete and the SSO feature will not work for your Organization members.
    </Message>
9. Click **Complete set up**.

Once setup is complete, members can log in via SAML.

<Message type="tip">
  You can test the connection by creating a member and logging in with the new member account.
</Message>

<Message type="important">
  Keep in mind that:
  - User mapping between Scaleway and the Identity Provider must be done on the username. When testing the connection, if an error persists about the user not existing in Scaleway, make sure your Identity Provider is mapping the user on their username.
  - Members need to already have been [created manually](/iam/principals/manage-members/#how-to-create-a-member) in Scaleway to log in.
  - If you delete a user in the IdP, the corresponding Member is not automatically deleted in your Scaleway Organization. The [deletion must happen manually](/iam/principals/manage-members/#how-to-delete-a-member).
</Message>


## Map user attributes

Scaleway matches Members using their username, received as the SAML `NameID` value, not their email address. Incorrect attribute mapping in the Identity Provider is a common cause of connection failures, where the Member cannot be found in Scaleway.

<Message type="important">
  The value sent as the SAML `NameID` must correspond to the username of the Member in Scaleway, not their email address, unless the two values happen to be identical. If a connection test fails with an error about the user not existing in Scaleway, check the attribute mapping in the Identity Provider first.
</Message>

### Google Workspace

On the **Attribute mapping** page of the Scaleway SAML app in Google Workspace, no additional mapping is generally required for SSO to work. Check that the following attributes are mapped as specified:

- Google Directory attribute: `Primary email` attribute under **Basic Information**
- SAML App attribute: `Username`

This mapping is often set by default. Click **Finish** to complete the app setup in Google Workspace.

<Message type="note">
  Despite its name, the `Primary email` attribute is mapped to the `Username` SAML attribute, not to `NameID`. Do not create a separate mapping to `NameID`.
</Message>

### Other identity providers

The mapping screen and terminology differ between providers, but the underlying rule stays the same: the attribute sent as `NameID` (or Subject) must contain the Scaleway username of the Member.

- For a full walkthrough with Authentik, see [How to set up SSO with Authentik](/iam/user-provisioning/set-up-sso-with-authentik/), which maps the `NameID` property to `Username`.
- For Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, OneLogin, or other providers, locate the `NameID` (or Subject) configuration of the SAML application, and map it to the attribute holding the username rather than the email address.

## Update the connection configuration

If you change your Identity Provider, you will need to re-configure your SAML connection.

1. Go to your security settings.
2. Scroll to the **Identity Federation** section.
3. Click **Edit configuration**. A pop-up appears.
4. (Optional) Replace the Identity Provider's Single Sign-On URL and Entity ID with the information of your new one.
5. Click **Confirm**.

## Add a certificate

If you started the connection set up, but did not add a certificate right away, you can add it after. While the certificate is not added, the connection between Scaleway and your Identity Provider will not be complete and the SSO feature will not work for your Organization members.

1. Go to your security settings.
2. Scroll to the **Identity Federation** section.
3. Click **+ Add certificate**. A pop-up appears.
4. Enter the signing certificate generated by your Identity Provider in the box.
5. Click **Confirm**.

## Renew a certificate

You must regularly update your signing certificate in the frequency set by your Identity Provider. To renew a certificate:

1. Go to your security settings.
2. Scroll to the **Identity Federation** section.
3. Click **Renew certificate**. A pop-up appears.
4. Enter the signing certificate generated by your Identity Provider in the box.
5. Click **Confirm**.

## Delete a connection

1. Go to your security settings.
2. Scroll to the **Identity Federation** section.
3. Click **Delete SSO**.
    <Message type="important">
      A pop-up appears to warn you that:
      - Deleting the connection will also delete your identity federation configuration and disable SAML-based SSO connections, preventing Members from logging in via this method. You can reconfigure identity federation at any time.
    </Message>
4. Type **DELETE** in the box to confirm.
5. Click **Delete**.

**Tu avais raison de me diriger vers la CLI : elle contient bien un véritable login navigateur avec retour automatique d’un jeton utilisateur.** Ma recherche précédente était insuffisante.

J’ai inspecté le dépôt à la révision `f4d37a5`, notamment :
- `internal/namespaces/login/login.go`
- `internal/namespaces/login/webcallback/webcallback.go`

### Le flux réel de `scw login`

```text
CLI démarre un serveur de callback local
  → ouvre https://account.scaleway.com/authenticate
      avec redirectToUrl=http://localhost:<port>/callback
  → l’utilisateur s’authentifie chez Scaleway
  → le navigateur revient au callback avec un paramètre token
  → la CLI décode une enveloppe Base64/JSON
      contenant token, renewToken et métadonnées jwt
  → initialise le SDK avec scw.WithJWT(token)
```

**Ce n’est donc pas une simple ouverture de la console suivie d’une saisie manuelle.** Le jeton revient automatiquement. En revanche, ce code ne montre pas un flux OAuth standard authorization-code/PKCE : il utilise un mécanisme Scaleway spécifique.

### Nuance importante
Après réception du JWT, la CLI appelle **`CreateAPIKey`**, puis configure son profil avec cette nouvelle clé. Elle utilise donc le jeton utilisateur pour amorcer une connexion durable par clé API.

Pour satisfaire **ton exigence sans clé API**, notre extension doit :
- reprendre le login navigateur et le callback ;
- **ne pas appeler `CreateAPIKey`** ;
- vérifier l’utilisation directe du JWT pour projets/modèles ;
- établir le renouvellement et l’expiration — `renewToken` est reçu, mais son utilisation n’est pas montrée dans ce parcours.

Le callback devra aussi être durci : loopback uniquement, contrôle du chemin, corrélation de la demande, délai et annulation, aucun jeton dans les logs. Je ne recopierai pas son écoute actuelle sur toutes les interfaces.

**Cette source donne enfin une base concrète pour le bon parcours.** Aucun fichier modifié et aucun login exécuté pendant cette inspection.

# 🚨 SESSION CLOSE PROTOCOL 🚨

**CRITICAL**: Before saying "done" or "complete", you MUST run this checklist:

```
[ ] bd close <id1> <id2> ...   (close completed issues)
```

**Note:** No git remote configured. Issues are saved locally only.

## Core Rules
- **Default**: Use beads for ALL task tracking (`bd create`, `bd ready`, `bd close`)
- **Prohibited**: Do NOT use TodoWrite, TaskCreate, or markdown files for task tracking
- **Workflow**: Create beads issue BEFORE writing code, mark in_progress when starting
- **Memory**: Use `bd remember "insight"` for persistent knowledge across sessions. Do NOT use MEMORY.md files — they fragment across accounts. Search with `bd memories <keyword>`.
- Persistence you don't need beats lost context
- Git authority: no git operations in this context
- Git workflow: local-only (no git remote)
- Session management: check `bd ready` for available work

## Essential Commands

### Finding Work
- `bd ready` - Show issues ready to work (no blockers)
- `bd list --status=open` - All open issues
- `bd list --status=in_progress` - Your active work
- `bd show <id>` - Detailed issue view with dependencies

### Creating & Updating
- `bd create --title="Summary of this issue" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task|bug|feature --priority=2` - New issue
  - Priority: 0-4 or P0-P4 (0=critical, 2=medium, 4=backlog). NOT "high"/"medium"/"low"
- `bd create ... --parent=<id>` - Hierarchical child (task under epic, subtask under task; inherits parent labels)
- `bd update <id> --claim` - Claim work
- `bd update <id> --assignee=username` - Assign to someone
- `bd update <id> --title/--description/--notes/--design` - Update fields inline
- `bd close <id>` - Mark complete
- `bd close <id1> <id2> ...` - Close multiple issues at once (more efficient)
- `bd close <id> --reason="explanation"` - Close with reason
- **Tip**: When creating multiple issues/tasks/epics, use parallel subagents for efficiency
- **WARNING**: Do NOT use `bd edit` - it opens $EDITOR (vim/nano) which blocks agents

### Dependencies & Blocking
- `bd dep add <issue> <depends-on>` - Add dependency (issue depends on depends-on)
- `bd blocked` - Show all blocked issues
- `bd show <id>` - See what's blocking/blocked by this issue

### Sync & Collaboration
- `bd search <query>` - Search issues by keyword

### Project Health
- `bd stats` - Project statistics (open/closed/blocked counts)
- `bd doctor` - Check for issues (sync problems, missing hooks)
- `bd doctor --check=conventions` - Check for convention drift (lint, stale, orphans)

### Quality Tools
- `bd create --validate` - Check description has required sections
- `bd create --acceptance="criteria"` - Set acceptance criteria (checked by --validate)
- `bd create --design="decisions"` - Record design decisions
- `bd create --notes="context"` - Add supplementary notes
- `bd config set validation.on-create warn` - Auto-validate on every create
- `bd lint` - Check existing issues for missing sections

### Lifecycle & Hygiene
- `bd defer <id> --until="date"` - Defer work to a future date
- `bd supersede <id> --with=<new-id>` - Mark issue as superseded
- `bd close <id> --suggest-next` - Show newly unblocked issues after closing
- `bd stale` - Find issues with no recent activity
- `bd orphans` - Find issues with broken dependencies
- `bd preflight` - Pre-PR checks (lint, stale, orphans)
- `bd human <id>` - Flag for human decision (list/respond/dismiss)

### Structured Workflows
- `bd formula list` - See available workflow templates
- `bd mol pour <name>` - Start structured workflow from formula

## Common Workflows

**Starting work:**
```bash
bd ready           # Find available work
bd show <id>       # Review issue details
bd update <id> --claim  # Claim it
```

**Completing work:**
```bash
bd close <id1> <id2> ...    # Close all completed issues at once
```

**Creating dependent work:**
```bash
# Run bd create commands in parallel (use subagents for many items)
bd create --title="Implement feature X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=feature
bd create --title="Write tests for X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task
bd dep add beads-yyy beads-xxx  # Tests depend on Feature (Feature blocks tests)
```

> **Note**: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are independent files (not symlinked and not sharing an inode). Mirror substantive edits across both, or symlink one to the other."

A community extension concept for discovering, testing, building, evaluating and deploying AI applications on Scaleway without leaving VS Code.

**Status:** experimental installable VS Code extension with native API-key connection/project switch and bounded read-only model discovery, plus separate offline streaming/cancel and experiment JSON. Real inference, full live-extension verification, production/design acceptance and cloud deployment remain separate gates. Name and branding are provisional; no official Scaleway affiliation is claimed.

Experimental community VS Code extension; no Scaleway affiliation. **User browser
login without API keys**, scoped read-only projects/dedicated deployments and a

## Install and try

    code --install-extension artifacts/scaleway-ai-toolkit-preview-0.0.7.vsix --force

Reload Window, then **Scaleway AI: Open Offline Preview** (legacy command name).

1. Mes ressources -> **Projet : sélectionner**, or **Se connecter à Scaleway**.
2. Confirm browser opening. Sign in on **account.scaleway.com**, not inside VS Code.
3. The browser returns the user JWT automatically to a temporary local callback.
   Return to VS Code; no token/password/key to copy or paste.
4. Enter the UUID of the organization you authorize for project reads. This is
   scope metadata, not a credential. Confirm up to 5 GET, then select a project.
5. Charger les modèles lists existing dedicated deployments of that project in
   **fr-par**, after a separate confirmation (up to 5 GET). No inference.

The UUID is still necessary to bound reads; automatic organization discovery is
not implemented. Browser credentials/MFA stay on Scaleway. The extension neither
creates an API key nor imports old keys. Successful login/disconnect deletes the
legacy preview API-key SecretStorage entry and connection metadata.

## Session and transport

Source-backed mechanism: Scaleway CLI login uses
https://account.scaleway.com/authenticate with redirectToUrl, receiving a Base64
JSON envelope with token/jwt/renewToken. We omit its subsequent CreateAPIKey step.
The SDK maps user JWT to **X-Session-Token**, not X-Auth-Token or Bearer for control
APIs. References and pinned hashes: evidence/documentation/scaleway-user-login-v1.json.
This is called **Scaleway user login**, not a verified OAuth authorization-code/
PKCE integration. No undocumented OAuth parameters or renewal endpoint invented.

JWT is retained **only in extension-host memory**, never in files, globalState,
SecretStorage, logs, webview, or chat. renewToken and browser metadata are discarded.
Shape and expiry are checked locally, not signature authenticity: the Scaleway API
validates authenticity and IAM on each request. Expiry is the earlier of JWT exp
and envelope expiresAt; session drops 30s before expiry. Reconnect after expiry,
Reload Window or extension restart. Disconnect clears the local session and cancels
pending work; it does **not** revoke the token or sign out of Scaleway in the browser.

Callback: IPv4 loopback only, OS-selected port, localhost redirect, random 192-bit
path correlation inside redirectToUrl, exact path/Host/peer/method, no Origin or
request body, bounded headers/query, one successful consumption, 3-minute timeout,
cancel and cleanup. No callback query/token logging. Success page has no-store,
no-referrer and nonce CSP and replaces the credential URL in browser history.
The provider's acceptance of the randomized localhost callback path remains to
be verified live; this is not a provider-verified state/PKCE guarantee. Like the
CLI flow, token arrives in a URL; localhost processes and browser machinery are
part of the trust boundary. Invalid callbacks do not consume the pending login.

**Local desktop VS Code only for browser login in this preview.** Remote SSH,
WSL, Containers and Codespaces hosts are blocked rather than opening an unusable
remote loopback callback. Workspace Trust required. Startup and tree navigation
make no API requests. A connected user session is not automatically permission
to run inference or mutate resources.

Control GET uses fixed api.scaleway.com routes, no retries/redirects/proxy env,
10s request deadline, 2MiB response limit, max5 sequential pages per collection.
No response body/header/error details logged; safe error codes only. A 401/403
drops the local session; check IAM/organization and reconnect, no key fallback.
Local minimum projections are not full production wire-schema validation.

**Serverless JWT audience/header support is not established.** This preview sends
no JWT to api.scaleway.ai and displays that limitation explicitly. No project/model
API acceptance has been verified with a real user account yet. Dedicated entries
are deployments, not the dedicated model catalog. Clicking a real entry shows
information only; **real models cannot run in this playground yet**.

Outils de développement -> Construire et tester -> **Playground modèle**.

JSON and save only if desired. Closing the panel cancels the demo. No prompt/output
automatically saved, no credentials passed to the webview, no API usage/billing.

# 🚨 SESSION CLOSE PROTOCOL 🚨

**CRITICAL**: Before saying "done" or "complete", you MUST run this checklist:

```
[ ] bd close <id1> <id2> ...   (close completed issues)
```

**Note:** No git remote configured. Issues are saved locally only.

## Core Rules
- **Default**: Use beads for ALL task tracking (`bd create`, `bd ready`, `bd close`)
- **Prohibited**: Do NOT use TodoWrite, TaskCreate, or markdown files for task tracking
- **Workflow**: Create beads issue BEFORE writing code, mark in_progress when starting
- **Memory**: Use `bd remember "insight"` for persistent knowledge across sessions. Do NOT use MEMORY.md files — they fragment across accounts. Search with `bd memories <keyword>`.
- Persistence you don't need beats lost context
- Git authority: no git operations in this context
- Git workflow: local-only (no git remote)
- Session management: check `bd ready` for available work

## Essential Commands

### Finding Work
- `bd ready` - Show issues ready to work (no blockers)
- `bd list --status=open` - All open issues
- `bd list --status=in_progress` - Your active work
- `bd show <id>` - Detailed issue view with dependencies

### Creating & Updating
- `bd create --title="Summary of this issue" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task|bug|feature --priority=2` - New issue
  - Priority: 0-4 or P0-P4 (0=critical, 2=medium, 4=backlog). NOT "high"/"medium"/"low"
- `bd create ... --parent=<id>` - Hierarchical child (task under epic, subtask under task; inherits parent labels)
- `bd update <id> --claim` - Claim work
- `bd update <id> --assignee=username` - Assign to someone
- `bd update <id> --title/--description/--notes/--design` - Update fields inline
- `bd close <id>` - Mark complete
- `bd close <id1> <id2> ...` - Close multiple issues at once (more efficient)
- `bd close <id> --reason="explanation"` - Close with reason
- **Tip**: When creating multiple issues/tasks/epics, use parallel subagents for efficiency
- **WARNING**: Do NOT use `bd edit` - it opens $EDITOR (vim/nano) which blocks agents

### Dependencies & Blocking
- `bd dep add <issue> <depends-on>` - Add dependency (issue depends on depends-on)
- `bd blocked` - Show all blocked issues
- `bd show <id>` - See what's blocking/blocked by this issue

### Sync & Collaboration
- `bd search <query>` - Search issues by keyword

### Project Health
- `bd stats` - Project statistics (open/closed/blocked counts)
- `bd doctor` - Check for issues (sync problems, missing hooks)
- `bd doctor --check=conventions` - Check for convention drift (lint, stale, orphans)

### Quality Tools
- `bd create --validate` - Check description has required sections
- `bd create --acceptance="criteria"` - Set acceptance criteria (checked by --validate)
- `bd create --design="decisions"` - Record design decisions
- `bd create --notes="context"` - Add supplementary notes
- `bd config set validation.on-create warn` - Auto-validate on every create
- `bd lint` - Check existing issues for missing sections

### Lifecycle & Hygiene
- `bd defer <id> --until="date"` - Defer work to a future date
- `bd supersede <id> --with=<new-id>` - Mark issue as superseded
- `bd close <id> --suggest-next` - Show newly unblocked issues after closing
- `bd stale` - Find issues with no recent activity
- `bd orphans` - Find issues with broken dependencies
- `bd preflight` - Pre-PR checks (lint, stale, orphans)
- `bd human <id>` - Flag for human decision (list/respond/dismiss)

### Structured Workflows
- `bd formula list` - See available workflow templates
- `bd mol pour <name>` - Start structured workflow from formula

## Common Workflows

**Starting work:**
```bash
bd ready           # Find available work
bd show <id>       # Review issue details
bd update <id> --claim  # Claim it
```

**Completing work:**
```bash
bd close <id1> <id2> ...    # Close all completed issues at once
```

**Creating dependent work:**
```bash
# Run bd create commands in parallel (use subagents for many items)
bd create --title="Implement feature X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=feature
bd create --title="Write tests for X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task
bd dep add beads-yyy beads-xxx  # Tests depend on Feature (Feature blocks tests)
```

content.text:
Oui pour la persistance, avec une distinction entre **secret** et **préférences**.

### 1. Conserver le JWT dans le trousseau système

Pour une extension VS Code, la bonne interface est **`ExtensionContext.secrets` — SecretStorage**.

Sous Linux, VS Code peut s’appuyer sur un trousseau compatible avec **freedesktop Secret Service**, comme GNOME Keyring, KWallet ou KeePassXC. Il ne faut pas écrire le JWT en clair dans un fichier sous `~/.config` : respecter les chemins XDG ne sécurise pas un secret.

**Attention au backend de VS Code :** l’option `password-store: basic` fournit seulement une obfuscation et n’est pas adaptée. Un backend tel que `gnome-libsecret` utilise Secret Service. SecretStorage ne permet pas à l’extension de garantir à lui seul quel backend est actif.

Le comportement recommandé serait :
- stocker le JWT et son expiration dans SecretStorage ;
- restaurer la session après redémarrage si elle est encore valide ;
- supprimer le secret expiré et relancer la connexion à la prochaine action ;
- supprimer le secret lors de la déconnexion.

**La persistance ne prolonge pas la durée du JWT.** Le renouvellement automatique reste à établir auprès de Scaleway.

### 2. Mémoriser l’organisation sélectionnée

Oui. Le **nom et l’UUID de l’organisation**, ainsi que le projet sélectionné, peuvent être conservés dans **`globalState`** de VS Code : ce sont des métadonnées, pas des identifiants d’authentification.

Parce que **le catalogue réel n’est pas encore correctement implémenté dans cette version**. La connexion fonctionne, mais j’ai laissé des entrées de menu qui donnent une impression de fonctionnalité plus complète qu’elle ne l’est.

| Entrée | Comportement actuel |
|---|---|
| **Catalogue de modèles** | Appelle la liste des déploiements dédiés, pas un véritable catalogue. C’est un mauvais raccordement de ma part. |
| **Serverless** | Aucun appel effectué : l’accès avec le JWT utilisateur n’est pas encore établi. La liste reste donc vide volontairement, mais l’interface devrait mieux l’expliquer. |
| **Déploiements dédiés** | Liste uniquement les déploiements **déjà créés dans le projet sélectionné, en `fr-par`**. Ce ne sont pas les modèles disponibles à déployer. |

Pour les déploiements dédiés, une liste vide peut donc être normale si aucun déploiement n’existe dans ce périmètre. **Je ne peux pas affirmer que c’est votre cas** sans distinguer le résultat réel d’une éventuelle erreur d’accès.

La correction nécessaire est de séparer clairement :
1. **Catalogue** : modèles proposés par Scaleway.
2. **Serverless** : modèles proposés en Serverless, avec disponibilité d’accès indiquée séparément.
3. **Déploiements dédiés** : ressources existantes de votre projet.

Le blocage de l’inférence Serverless par JWT ne devrait pas empêcher d’afficher un catalogue obtenu par une autre route officielle vérifiée. **Je ne vous demanderai pas de clé API pour contourner cela.**

### Structure cible pour Scaleway

```text
Mes ressources
├── Définir le projet Scaleway
├── Modèles
│   ├── Serverless
│   └── Déploiements dédiés
├── Agents                         [phase avancée]
├── Outils                         [à implémenter]
├── Connaissances                  [à implémenter]
├── Évaluations                    [à implémenter]
├── Récents
└── Ressources locales

Outils de développement
├── Découvrir
│   ├── Catalogue de modèles
│   └── Catalogue d’outils         [à implémenter]
├── Construire
│   ├── Créer un agent             [phase avancée]
│   ├── Inspecteur d’agent         [phase avancée]
│   ├── Déployer sur Scaleway      [à implémenter]
│   ├── Playground agent          [phase avancée]
│   └── Playground modèle
└── Surveiller                     [à implémenter]

Aide et retours
```

**Distinction importante :**
- **Mes ressources → Modèles** concerne les modèles utilisables et les déploiements du projet.
- **Découvrir → Catalogue de modèles** présente les offres Scaleway à explorer, indépendamment des ressources déjà créées.
- La démonstration synthétique actuelle devrait rejoindre **Ressources locales**, plutôt qu’occuper une place centrale parmi les ressources cloud.

### Sélecteur de projet

L’entrée **Définir le projet Scaleway** devrait ouvrir :

- **Changer de projet** → connexion si nécessaire → organisation → projet → mémorisation comme projet par défaut.
- **Créer un projet** → création puis définition comme projet par défaut.

La création est une **écriture cloud** : elle nécessite une implémentation dédiée avec confirmation explicite. Elle n’est pas disponible actuellement.

Je ne reprendrai pas **Classic**, conversion de modèles ou fine-tuning sans équivalent Scaleway pertinent. Les fonctionnalités non implémentées ci-dessus décrivent la cible : elles ne doivent pas apparaître comme des actions fonctionnelles vides dans le VSIX.

**L’écart actuel à corriger est donc surtout l’organisation : rapprocher les ressources, la découverte et la construction de ce parcours, tout en conservant la connexion automatique et les lectures silencieuses déjà ajoutées.**

# Wayland Desktop Capture

## Objective

Produce inspectable screenshots of the real desktop state under Wayland and compare visible results against explicit expectations. Prefer the desktop portal on GNOME because shell, X11, and compositor-specific capture tools may be unavailable or denied.

## Mandatory workflow

### 1. Calibrate once

Record the session and available mechanisms:

```bash
printf 'DISPLAY=%s WAYLAND_DISPLAY=%s XDG_SESSION_TYPE=%s XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=%s' "$DISPLAY" "$WAYLAND_DISPLAY" "$XDG_SESSION_TYPE" "$XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP"
command -v grim gnome-screenshot spectacle import scrot 2>/dev/null || true
```

Do not repeatedly retry an incompatible mechanism. On GNOME Wayland, use the portal default below. On wlroots compositors, `grim` may be the shortest path. X11 tools such as ImageMagick `import`, `scrot`, `wmctrl`, and `xdotool` are not reliable evidence for native Wayland windows.

### 2. Capture through the GNOME/Wayland portal

Run the bundled script rather than recreating D-Bus synchronization:

```bash
python3 scripts/portal_screenshot.py --output /absolute/path/to/evidence.png --timeout 20
```

The script keeps one D-Bus connection alive until `org.freedesktop.portal.Request.Response` arrives. This matters because a one-shot `gdbus call` exits before the asynchronous portal response. The portal may show a user confirmation dialog; this is expected security behavior.

Prerequisites: Python 3, `dbus-python`, PyGObject, a running desktop portal, and an interactive graphical session. If any are unavailable, report capture as **blocked** with the failed prerequisite. Never claim visual verification from source code alone.

### 3. Stabilize before capture

After the action that changes the UI, first ensure the target window is foregrounded. The portal captures the desktop, not a requested application; a valid PNG of another foreground window is not evidence about the target. Wait for rendering and loading to settle. Use a bounded delay, normally 1–2 seconds, then capture. For loading indicators or asynchronous assets, take an initial screenshot and a second screenshot after the documented timeout.

### 4. Inspect the image

Use the image-reading capability on the saved absolute path. Check visible headings, selected navigation, loading/error states, clipping, overlap, unexpected selection overlays, and whether the intended application is actually on screen. A successful PNG write proves capture only, not UI correctness.

### 5. Compare against explicit expectations

Record one row per action:

| Action | Expected visible state | Observed visible state | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| tool or interaction | concrete heading/navigation/state | evidence from screenshot | pass/fail/blocked |

Use **pass** only when the screenshot visibly supports the expectation. If the expected application is absent, another window is foregrounded, or the result remains on a default page, use **fail**, not pass.

### 6. Preserve evidence

Store screenshots and a short Markdown report in the project audit directory. Use stable descriptive names such as `01-before.png`, `02-after-action.png`, and `README.md`. Include resolution, capture method, expected-versus-observed results, and any environment limitation.

## Known failure signatures

- `grim: compositor doesn't support the screen capture protocol`: compositor is not exposing wlroots screencopy; switch to the portal.
- GNOME Shell `Screenshot is not allowed`: direct Shell D-Bus API is denied to the caller; switch to the portal.
- One-shot portal call returns only a request object path: the caller exited before the asynchronous response; run the bundled persistent script.
- `import -window root` fails or sees no windows: XWayland tools cannot capture native Wayland surfaces; do not keep retrying X11 tools.
- Synthetic keyboard tools report unsupported virtual keyboard protocol: do not depend on injecting Print Screen; use the portal.

## Verification gate

A desktop verification is complete only when:

1. the screenshot exists and has plausible nonzero dimensions;
2. the image has been inspected, not merely generated;
3. observed content is compared with a stated expectation;
4. failures remain failures in the report;

Publishing is a separate and higher-risk capability than installing a package. Never infer publish permission from successful private-package reads.

# 🚨 SESSION CLOSE PROTOCOL 🚨

**CRITICAL**: Before saying "done" or "complete", you MUST run this checklist:

```
[ ] bd close <id1> <id2> ...   (close completed issues)
```

**Note:** No git remote configured. Issues are saved locally only.

## Core Rules
- **Default**: Use beads for ALL task tracking (`bd create`, `bd ready`, `bd close`)
- **Prohibited**: Do NOT use TodoWrite, TaskCreate, or markdown files for task tracking
- **Workflow**: Create beads issue BEFORE writing code, mark in_progress when starting
- **Memory**: Use `bd remember "insight"` for persistent knowledge across sessions. Do NOT use MEMORY.md files — they fragment across accounts. Search with `bd memories <keyword>`.
- Persistence you don't need beats lost context
- Git authority: no git operations in this context
- Git workflow: local-only (no git remote)
- Session management: check `bd ready` for available work

## Essential Commands

### Finding Work
- `bd ready` - Show issues ready to work (no blockers)
- `bd list --status=open` - All open issues
- `bd list --status=in_progress` - Your active work
- `bd show <id>` - Detailed issue view with dependencies

### Creating & Updating
- `bd create --title="Summary of this issue" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task|bug|feature --priority=2` - New issue
  - Priority: 0-4 or P0-P4 (0=critical, 2=medium, 4=backlog). NOT "high"/"medium"/"low"
- `bd create ... --parent=<id>` - Hierarchical child (task under epic, subtask under task; inherits parent labels)
- `bd update <id> --claim` - Claim work
- `bd update <id> --assignee=username` - Assign to someone
- `bd update <id> --title/--description/--notes/--design` - Update fields inline
- `bd close <id>` - Mark complete
- `bd close <id1> <id2> ...` - Close multiple issues at once (more efficient)
- `bd close <id> --reason="explanation"` - Close with reason
- **Tip**: When creating multiple issues/tasks/epics, use parallel subagents for efficiency
- **WARNING**: Do NOT use `bd edit` - it opens $EDITOR (vim/nano) which blocks agents

### Dependencies & Blocking
- `bd dep add <issue> <depends-on>` - Add dependency (issue depends on depends-on)
- `bd blocked` - Show all blocked issues
- `bd show <id>` - See what's blocking/blocked by this issue

### Sync & Collaboration
- `bd search <query>` - Search issues by keyword

### Project Health
- `bd stats` - Project statistics (open/closed/blocked counts)
- `bd doctor` - Check for issues (sync problems, missing hooks)
- `bd doctor --check=conventions` - Check for convention drift (lint, stale, orphans)

### Quality Tools
- `bd create --validate` - Check description has required sections
- `bd create --acceptance="criteria"` - Set acceptance criteria (checked by --validate)
- `bd create --design="decisions"` - Record design decisions
- `bd create --notes="context"` - Add supplementary notes
- `bd config set validation.on-create warn` - Auto-validate on every create
- `bd lint` - Check existing issues for missing sections

### Lifecycle & Hygiene
- `bd defer <id> --until="date"` - Defer work to a future date
- `bd supersede <id> --with=<new-id>` - Mark issue as superseded
- `bd close <id> --suggest-next` - Show newly unblocked issues after closing
- `bd stale` - Find issues with no recent activity
- `bd orphans` - Find issues with broken dependencies
- `bd preflight` - Pre-PR checks (lint, stale, orphans)
- `bd human <id>` - Flag for human decision (list/respond/dismiss)

### Structured Workflows
- `bd formula list` - See available workflow templates
- `bd mol pour <name>` - Start structured workflow from formula

## Common Workflows

**Starting work:**
```bash
bd ready           # Find available work
bd show <id>       # Review issue details
bd update <id> --claim  # Claim it
```

**Completing work:**
```bash
bd close <id1> <id2> ...    # Close all completed issues at once
```

**Creating dependent work:**
```bash
# Run bd create commands in parallel (use subagents for many items)
bd create --title="Implement feature X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=feature
bd create --title="Write tests for X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task
bd dep add beads-yyy beads-xxx  # Tests depend on Feature (Feature blocks tests)
```

        encoded,

Use Beads as the shared project task system. Local plans, scratch files, and personal memories are useful, but they are not the durable source of truth for project work.

bd prime

bd where

## Preferred Route

Use the `bd` CLI when shell access is available. It is the most compact and direct Beads interface.

## Core CLI Workflow

1. Find work:

```bash
bd ready
bd list --status=open
bd list --status=in_progress
```

2. Inspect before editing:

```bash
bd show <id>
```

3. Claim work atomically:

```bash
bd update <id> --claim
```

4. Create durable follow-up work when implementation reveals new tasks:

```bash
bd create "Short title" --description="Why this exists and what needs to be done" --type=task --priority=2
```

5. Close completed work:

```bash
bd close <id> --reason="Completed"
```

## What Belongs In Beads

Use Beads for:

- shared project tasks
- blockers and dependencies
- discovered follow-up work
- work that must survive thread reset, compaction, or handoff
- status that another person or agent should be able to resume

    '',

# Portable contracts v1

Owner: Beads .1.5. Normative design for advanced execution; not a server,
production validator or release approval. JSON Schema Draft 7; exact envelope
version 1.0.0. Contracts are ours, separate from provider/OpenAI/Strands types.

## Files and ownership

- agent-spec/v1/schema.json: saved configuration, not authority.
- runtime-http/v1/schema.json: typed request/response bodies, not all authorization checks.
- runtime-events/v1/schema.json: safe runtime-origin events.
- webview-ipc/v1/schema.json: reference-only host/webview action slice.
- fixtures/: synthetic examples and invalid/sequence cases consumed in both languages.
- [Architecture ADR](../specifications/decisions/0004-runtime-contracts.md).
- [Operational protocol](../specifications/runtime-protocol.md).

## Validation requirements

Closed objects reject unknown properties/versions. Local-only schema references;
no remote resolution. Application additionally enforces max JSON body 256 KiB,
event 32 KiB, JSON depth 32, duplicate-key/nonfinite rejection, integer-safe values,
UTF-8 and recursively sanitized serialization. Schema validates shape, not secret
absence, grants, endpoint trust, causal event order, known capabilities, ledger
atomicity or truthful outcomes. Opaque references resolve only through trusted
host/runtime registries, never workspace-provided URL/environment/command data.

Spec revision is SHA256 of canonical UTF-8 JSON excluding its own revision field;
object keys sorted lexicographically, no whitespace, NFC strings, arrays retain
order, finite numbers represented per RFC 8785/JCS. Implementations must use an
actual JCS implementation, not ordinary JSON.stringify; fixtures use placeholder
digests and do not prove digest computation. Scope/data/tool/model revisions have
separate canonical inputs. Reject inconsistent digests before effects.

Exact version negotiation: v1.0.0 only initially. Unknown major/minor/patch is
unsupported_version until both sides explicitly advertise and test it. No silent
migration. Future additions require new version and conformance fixtures; historical
schemas/examples remain unchanged. Existing spec edits require diff/review, never
silent overwrite or auto-execution after migration.

## Shared model target

serverless model_id is discovery identifier; dedicated catalog_model_ref,
deployment_ref, endpoint_ref and inference_model_id are distinct. The same model
reference can serve model playground and advanced agents. Endpoint references are
not URLs or permissions. Scope refs resolve distinct org/project values even when
provider IDs happen to match. fr-par is the currently reviewed scope, not a promise
that the provider can never support more regions.

max_output_tokens maps to verified Chat Completions max_tokens; unknown feature or
unsupported sampling parameter is a validation error, not silently filtered.
No native structured_output/provider parse baseline. prompt_json_local_validation
max_retries=5/max_physical_sends=6 is a ceiling within the same smaller parent budget;
transport retries consume it, and correction sends cannot use tools/replay the agent.

## Tool and content boundary

Specs carry tool/config/schema references only. Executable/config/argument effect
classification and grants come from trusted registries and host review, not model
text or file declarations. Raw args/results are not event bodies: immutable revisions
and approved result refs permit separately controlled inspection. text.delta is
untrusted, sanitized content for explicitly consented display only; no automatic
trace/session persistence. An event may never cause tool dispatch.

IPC initial slice routes intents by immutable content/selection references. Editable
prompt/agent document transport is intentionally not exposed here: host-owned text
editors/content registry create revisions under approved workspace reads. A future
webview edit transport must add a separately versioned bounded content contract;
this schema is not a complete Agent Builder UI or mandatory chat interface.

# Product specification

Revision 0.1 — 2026-10-20. Proposed baseline derived from the stakeholder goal and initial analysis. Product authority: [vision](../PRODUCT.md#vision). Status lives in Beads, not this document.

<a id="requirements"></a>
## Requirements and acceptance

### R01 — Connection and scope (MVP)
Use VS Code SecretStorage for credential material; store only safe connection references in workspace configuration. Display connection, project and region where relevant. Distinguish serverless inference scope from regional dedicated resources. Test invalid/revoked credentials and least-privilege IAM. Acceptance: switching connection cannot reuse another connection's cached resources or pending result; secrets never enter webview messages, exports or logs.

### R02 — Catalog and capabilities (MVP)
Discover actual available models through verified provider contracts, not a hardcoded marketing list. Support pagination/cache freshness and accurate unavailable states. Represent streaming, tool calls, structured outputs, images, embeddings and usage as supported/unsupported/unknown with provenance. Acceptance: unavailable discovery is not an empty-success list; unknown capabilities do not unlock dependent controls; endpoint changes invalidate stale capability data.

### R03 — Playground (MVP)
Select a supported model, edit system/user messages and supported parameters, stream a response, cancel and retry safely. Keep pending runs bound to their originating connection/model/prompt revision. Handle partial output, throttling, network failure and unsupported parameters. Acceptance: cancellation stops local processing and reports provider cancellation uncertainty honestly; late output does not replace another experiment; region/data destination remains visible before send. Multimodal inputs are deferred until capabilities and data consent are verified.

### R04 — Save and export (MVP)
Version saved prompt/settings without credentials; export runnable Python and TypeScript examples using external secret references. Acceptance: exported code runs outside the extension; existing files and manual edits require diff/review before overwrite; saved, generated and actually executed states are distinct.

### R05 — Resource browsing (MVP)
Read-only dedicated deployment and endpoint views filtered to selected project/region, with refresh, pagination and permission/error states. Acceptance: changing scope invalidates stale results; no create/update/delete side effect from navigation; last-known status is labeled stale during failed refresh.

### R06 — Portable agent specification (phase 2)
Versioned validated specification for connection reference, prompt, parameters, output schema, tools, retrieval, runtime and evaluations. Acceptance: round-trip read/write and schema validation tests, unsupported-version errors, no embedded secrets, and existing edits preserved.

### R07 — Local runtime and tools (phase 2)
Stakeholder-selected Strands Python SDK inside a thin HTTP runtime; reuse its agent loop with verified pre-effect policy hooks, bounded execution, timeouts, cancellation and normalized events. Explicit Scaleway transport/external credentials; no provider fallback or duplicate custom orchestration loop. MCP server launch requires Workspace Trust and explicit approved configuration. Acceptance: injected tool output cannot grant authority; budgets/steps enforced; revocation stops new actions; unknown external effects are reconciled before retry; untrusted projects cannot execute workspace code.

### R07a — Validated JSON output and bounded correction
Accepted baseline: [ADR 0003](decisions/0003-prompt-json-bounded-repair.md). Request JSON through ordinary model calls, parse strictly and validate locally; native Strands structured_output/provider parse shortcuts disabled. Each parse/schema failure supplies normalized, redacted and bounded errors plus the fixed schema and safe previous output for model-only correction. max_retries=5 means six logical attempts maximum; all physical sends including transport retries share a six-send ceiling and parent budgets. No tools or entire agent rerun during repair. Stop on policy/auth/budget/revocation/cancellation/unknown effects; exhaustion is explicit failure, never invalid-output success. Acceptance: deterministic offline tests cover corrected feedback, sixth-send success/exhaustion, no seventh send, strict local-only validation, secret-safe errors, budget/revocation and no native path/tool dispatch; actual Strands guards/live compatibility remain separate checks.

### R08 — Inspector and evaluation (phase 2)
Correlate model/tool events, timings, errors and run identifiers. Dataset evaluation supports versioned cases, deterministic metrics and optional clearly labeled model judges. Acceptance: cancelled/partial/error runs excluded from success totals or explicitly labeled; traces redact secrets and minimize payloads; evaluation concurrency/spend bounded; metrics and judge provenance recorded.

### R09 — Dedicated model deployment (phase 3)
Wizard backed by verified models/node types, permissions and regional availability. Review resources, network exposure, estimated-versus-unknown cost and model EULA before activation. Acceptance: no automatic EULA acceptance; asynchronous state polling, partial-failure reconciliation and cleanup; destructive operations require explicit reviewed scope.

### R10 — Hosted agent application (phase 3)
Package runtime/application, build image, push to selected registry and deploy to validated hosting target. Serverless Containers is a candidate, not guaranteed; persistent sessions must be externalized. Acceptance: deployment contract documents HTTP/streaming duration, state and networking limits; created resource IDs retained; failed provisioning recoverable without blind duplication; hosted playground uses same event protocol as local inspector.

### R11 — Monitoring and cleanup (phase 3)
Provide deployment status/logs and local traces; validate Cockpit trace integration separately. Acceptance: provider acceptance not reported as proven healthy runtime; trace links retain run/project scope; owned-resource cleanup and failure reconciliation tested; no mandatory collection of prompts or documents.

### R12 — Accessibility, security and operational quality (all phases)
VS Code light/dark/high-contrast themes; keyboard-first navigation, descriptive labels, correct focus and zoom. Extension/webview IPC typed and validated, restrictive CSP, output sanitization, least privilege, consent before transmitting workspace data, no unsolicited telemetry. Acceptance: automated tests plus rendered keyboard/theme checks; no untreated critical/high security issue; release build/package tested only under separate release authorization.

<a id="release-slices"></a>
## Release slice boundaries

MVP ends at exported runnable model example and read-only dedicated resources. It does not promise a deployed agent. Phase 2 ends at reproducible local tool-using agent and comparable evaluations. Phase 3 ends at hosted application inspected and removable. Advanced work stays research/backlog until evidence justifies it.

<a id="quality-evidence"></a>
## Required verification evidence

Record unit/integration coverage, fixture versus live-test provenance, model capability versions, error/recovery cases, secret scanning, visual-source approvals where applicable and runtime/deployment evidence. Real account tests require an authorized account and budget; absent access is a blocker, not a passed test. UI approval and prototype QA cannot prove user value or production authorization.


### Stakeholder clarification — 2026-10-20

Agent creation, editing and execution are advanced phase 2 functions, not an MVP
prerequisite. Foundry Toolkit is a workflow reference, not an assumed exact feature
inventory. The model-only MVP must work without installing or starting the Strands
Python agent runtime; Python code export does not imply a Python runtime dependency
for the extension itself. Prepare versioned advanced contracts in .1.5, but do not
add agent onboarding, mandatory agent configuration or agent placeholders to the
basic model journey. Advanced authoring/execution remains separately approved.

## Stakeholder functional reference

See [Foundry Toolkit capability mapping](functional-reference-foundry.md) for official stakeholder references, observed features, Scaleway equivalents and deferred scope. Reproduce developer outcomes, not proprietary implementation or Azure service contracts.

## Accepted delivery sequence — 2026-10-20

Stakeholder confirms: model MVP -> dedicated model deployment (.5.1) -> advanced
local agents (.4.1 onward) -> optional hosted application. Keep existing IDs/phase
labels as historical grouping; the dependency graph carries the approved order.
Serverless remains usable without dedicated deployment. No writes/spend implied.

pour information zur le toolkit azure foundry que l'on utilise pour inspiration:
Pour **Foundry Toolkit dans VS Code**, je regrouperais les possibilités en **huit parcours utilisateurs**, selon l’objectif recherché. Ils peuvent s’enchaîner : on commence par tester un modèle, puis on construit un agent, on l’évalue et on le déploie.

L’interface distingue **My Resources**, pour retrouver les ressources existantes, et **Developer Tools**, pour lancer les actions de développement. [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/get-started-projects-vs-code?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**1. « Je veux choisir un modèle et tester une idée »**

C’est le parcours d’exploration, avant de développer une application.

1. Ouvrir **Model Catalog**.
2. Choisir où faire tourner le modèle : Foundry, fournisseur externe, ou environnement local.
3. Déployer, connecter ou télécharger le modèle selon cette destination.
4. L’ouvrir dans **Model Playground**.
5. Tester des demandes, modifier les paramètres et comparer les réponses.

**Exemple :** comparer deux modèles sur leur capacité à résumer un incident technique.

**Résultat :** un modèle accessible et une première appréciation de son comportement. Le catalogue permet aussi de connecter un endpoint compatible personnalisé, notamment sur un réseau privé. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/models?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**2. « Je veux prototyper un agent sur mon poste »**

Ce parcours passe par **Agent Builder**, avec une configuration sauvegardée localement.

1. Sélectionner un modèle.
2. Écrire les instructions de l’agent.
3. Ajouter éventuellement des outils MCP.
4. Configurer une sortie structurée, si le modèle la supporte.
5. Tester les conversations et enregistrer les versions locales.
6. Générer du code d’intégration pour poursuivre le développement.

**Exemple :** extraire d’un compte rendu un JSON contenant les décisions et les actions.

**Résultat :** une configuration locale réutilisable. **Le modèle peut être distant même lorsque la configuration est locale.** [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/agentbuilder?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**3. « Je veux un agent géré dans Foundry, principalement par configuration »**

On utilise ici un **prompt agent** : son comportement repose sur un modèle, des instructions et des outils supportés par le service.

1. Se connecter à Azure et sélectionner un projet Foundry.
2. Créer l’agent dans **Agent Builder**.
3. Choisir le modèle et définir ses instructions.
4. Ajouter les outils nécessaires.
5. Tester puis sauvegarder une version dans Foundry.
6. Générer du code client pour l’appeler depuis une application.

**Exemple :** un assistant de support qui recherche dans une documentation avant de répondre.

**Résultat :** un agent versionné dans Foundry, utilisable par une application. **Sauvegarder sa version et publier une application avec un endpoint stable sont deux opérations distinctes.** [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/agentbuilder?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Le choix entre les deux principales formes d’agent se fait ainsi :

| Question | Prompt agent | Hosted agent |
|---|---|---|
| Comment définir son comportement ? | Instructions et configuration des outils | Code et orchestration personnalisée |
| Que maintient l’équipe ? | Configuration, intégrations et évaluations | Code, dépendances, packaging et évaluations |
| Quand le choisir ? | Les capacités configurables couvrent le besoin | Le besoin exige une logique d’exécution spécifique |

**Les deux peuvent servir une application en production**, après les validations nécessaires. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/create-agents?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**4. « Je veux développer mon agent en code et l’héberger dans Foundry »**

C’est le parcours **Hosted Agent**.

1. Ouvrir **Create Agent**.
2. Partir d’un exemple : Agent Framework, Copilot SDK, LangGraph ou autre exemple disponible.
3. Générer le projet dans son workspace.
4. Développer sa logique et installer ses dépendances.
5. Exécuter et déboguer l’agent localement.
6. Lancer **Deploy to Microsoft Foundry**.
7. Déployer le code en ZIP ou une image de conteneur via ACR.
8. Tester l’agent distant dans le **Hosted Agent Playground**.

**Exemple :** un traitement qui analyse une demande, appelle plusieurs services puis construit une réponse selon des règles métier.

**Résultat :** du **code source dans ton dépôt**, exécuté dans une infrastructure gérée par Foundry. Tu conserves la responsabilité du code et de ses dépendances ; Foundry prend en charge l’hébergement et la mise à l’échelle. Ce parcours est documenté en préversion. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/hosted-agents?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Une variante consiste à utiliser **GitHub Copilot en mode Agent** pour générer ou modifier le code, ajouter des évaluations ou instrumenter les traces avec les outils spécialisés du Toolkit. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/copilot-tools?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**5. « Je veux connecter mon agent aux données et aux actions métier »**

Ce parcours enrichit un agent existant.

1. Ouvrir **Tool Catalog**.
2. Choisir une capacité ou renseigner une connexion personnalisée.
3. Configurer l’endpoint et l’authentification.
4. Attacher les outils à l’agent, directement ou via une **Toolbox**.
5. Tester une demande qui nécessite réellement l’appel de l’outil.

**Exemple :** rechercher un incident dans un service interne puis récupérer sa documentation associée.

Les mécanismes ont des rôles différents :

| Mécanisme | Usage |
|---|---|
| **MCP** | Exposer des outils à l’agent |
| **OpenAPI** | Décrire les opérations d’une API HTTP |
| **A2A** | Connecter un agent à un autre |
| **Toolbox** | Regrouper et partager un ensemble versionné d’outils et de skills |

**Résultat :** un agent capable d’interagir avec son environnement. Une connexion MCP configurée sur ton poste doit être rendue accessible et authentifiée pour être utilisable depuis un agent cloud. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/tool-catalog?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**6. « Je veux mesurer la qualité et détecter les régressions »**

Le Toolkit propose plusieurs chemins selon ce que tu possèdes déjà :

| Point de départ | Parcours |
|---|---|
| Des réponses déjà enregistrées | Importer un dataset et calculer leurs scores |
| Un prompt local à améliorer | Exécuter les mêmes cas dans la grille d’évaluation d’Agent Builder |
| Un agent avec des critères d’acceptation | Générer des tests Python avec **pytest** |
| Un agent Foundry à évaluer dans le service | Préparer une évaluation Foundry, éventuellement avec Copilot |

**Exemple :** rejouer 100 demandes représentatives pour vérifier qu’un changement de modèle conserve la pertinence des réponses et la bonne utilisation des outils.

**Résultat :** des mesures comparables entre versions et, avec les tests, des critères de réussite explicites. L’évaluation peut s’exécuter localement tout en appelant des modèles ou agents distants. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/evaluation?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**7. « Je veux comprendre pourquoi mon agent échoue ou ralentit »**

Deux parcours complémentaires répondent à ce besoin :

- **Agent Inspector** : lancer une requête sur un agent local, examiner les appels d’outils et utiliser des points d’arrêt dans son code. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/agent-inspector?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
- **Tracing** : analyser les opérations enregistrées, leurs durées et leurs erreurs. Les traces locales passent par un collecteur OpenTelemetry ; celles des hosted agents sont consultées via l’Application Insights associé au projet. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/tracing?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Exemple :** déterminer si les dix secondes d’attente viennent du modèle, d’une API ou d’une succession d’appels.

**Résultat :** identifier l’étape responsable et vérifier l’effet d’une correction.

**8. « Je veux adapter ou optimiser un modèle »**

Ce parcours s’adresse davantage aux profils ML et aux développeurs d’applications exécutant des modèles sur les appareils.

- **Conversion et quantification** : partir d’un modèle supporté, le convertir en ONNX, réduire sa précision et évaluer le résultat pour une exécution locale sur CPU, GPU ou NPU, dans les environnements Windows pris en charge. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/modelconversion?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
- **Fine-tuning** : préparer des données d’apprentissage et de test, entraîner une adaptation puis mesurer son intérêt. Un parcours documenté concerne notamment les adaptateurs LoRA de Phi Silica. [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/intelligentapps/finetune?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Exemple :** adapter un modèle à un format de réponse spécialisé, ou réduire ses besoins matériels pour une application locale.

**Résultat :** un modèle optimisé ou un adaptateur entraîné, à intégrer ensuite dans l’application.

# 🚨 SESSION CLOSE PROTOCOL 🚨

**CRITICAL**: Before saying "done" or "complete", you MUST run this checklist:

```
[ ] bd close <id1> <id2> ...   (close completed issues)
```

**Note:** No git remote configured. Issues are saved locally only.

## Core Rules
- **Default**: Use beads for ALL task tracking (`bd create`, `bd ready`, `bd close`)
- **Prohibited**: Do NOT use TodoWrite, TaskCreate, or markdown files for task tracking
- **Workflow**: Create beads issue BEFORE writing code, mark in_progress when starting
- **Memory**: Use `bd remember "insight"` for persistent knowledge across sessions. Do NOT use MEMORY.md files — they fragment across accounts. Search with `bd memories <keyword>`.
- Persistence you don't need beats lost context
- Git authority: no git operations in this context
- Git workflow: local-only (no git remote)
- Session management: check `bd ready` for available work

## Essential Commands

### Finding Work
- `bd ready` - Show issues ready to work (no blockers)
- `bd list --status=open` - All open issues
- `bd list --status=in_progress` - Your active work
- `bd show <id>` - Detailed issue view with dependencies

### Creating & Updating
- `bd create --title="Summary of this issue" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task|bug|feature --priority=2` - New issue
  - Priority: 0-4 or P0-P4 (0=critical, 2=medium, 4=backlog). NOT "high"/"medium"/"low"
- `bd create ... --parent=<id>` - Hierarchical child (task under epic, subtask under task; inherits parent labels)
- `bd update <id> --claim` - Claim work
- `bd update <id> --assignee=username` - Assign to someone
- `bd update <id> --title/--description/--notes/--design` - Update fields inline
- `bd close <id>` - Mark complete
- `bd close <id1> <id2> ...` - Close multiple issues at once (more efficient)
- `bd close <id> --reason="explanation"` - Close with reason
- **Tip**: When creating multiple issues/tasks/epics, use parallel subagents for efficiency
- **WARNING**: Do NOT use `bd edit` - it opens $EDITOR (vim/nano) which blocks agents

### Dependencies & Blocking
- `bd dep add <issue> <depends-on>` - Add dependency (issue depends on depends-on)
- `bd blocked` - Show all blocked issues
- `bd show <id>` - See what's blocking/blocked by this issue

### Sync & Collaboration
- `bd search <query>` - Search issues by keyword

### Project Health
- `bd stats` - Project statistics (open/closed/blocked counts)
- `bd doctor` - Check for issues (sync problems, missing hooks)
- `bd doctor --check=conventions` - Check for convention drift (lint, stale, orphans)

### Quality Tools
- `bd create --validate` - Check description has required sections
- `bd create --acceptance="criteria"` - Set acceptance criteria (checked by --validate)
- `bd create --design="decisions"` - Record design decisions
- `bd create --notes="context"` - Add supplementary notes
- `bd config set validation.on-create warn` - Auto-validate on every create
- `bd lint` - Check existing issues for missing sections

### Lifecycle & Hygiene
- `bd defer <id> --until="date"` - Defer work to a future date
- `bd supersede <id> --with=<new-id>` - Mark issue as superseded
- `bd close <id> --suggest-next` - Show newly unblocked issues after closing
- `bd stale` - Find issues with no recent activity
- `bd orphans` - Find issues with broken dependencies
- `bd preflight` - Pre-PR checks (lint, stale, orphans)
- `bd human <id>` - Flag for human decision (list/respond/dismiss)

### Structured Workflows
- `bd formula list` - See available workflow templates
- `bd mol pour <name>` - Start structured workflow from formula

## Common Workflows

**Starting work:**
```bash
bd ready           # Find available work
bd show <id>       # Review issue details
bd update <id> --claim  # Claim it
```

**Completing work:**
```bash
bd close <id1> <id2> ...    # Close all completed issues at once
```

**Creating dependent work:**
```bash
# Run bd create commands in parallel (use subagents for many items)
bd create --title="Implement feature X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=feature
bd create --title="Write tests for X" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task
bd dep add beads-yyy beads-xxx  # Tests depend on Feature (Feature blocks tests)
```

Captures and visually verifies live desktop UI on Linux Wayland, especially GNOME, using the screenshot portal when compositor-native or X11 tools fail. Use for screenshots, visual regression evidence, MCP App verification, or expected-versus-observed desktop UI checks under Wayland.

## Content

# Wayland Desktop Capture

## Objective

Produce inspectable screenshots of the real desktop state under Wayland and compare visible results against explicit expectations. Prefer the desktop portal on GNOME because shell, X11, and compositor-specific capture tools may be unavailable or denied.

## Mandatory workflow

### 1. Calibrate once

Record the session and available mechanisms:

```bash
printf 'DISPLAY=%s WAYLAND_DISPLAY=%s XDG_SESSION_TYPE=%s XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=%s' "$DISPLAY" "$WAYLAND_DISPLAY" "$XDG_SESSION_TYPE" "$XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP"
command -v grim gnome-screenshot spectacle import scrot 2>/dev/null || true
```

Do not repeatedly retry an incompatible mechanism. On GNOME Wayland, use the portal default below. On wlroots compositors, `grim` may be the shortest path. X11 tools such as ImageMagick `import`, `scrot`, `wmctrl`, and `xdotool` are not reliable evidence for native Wayland windows.

### 2. Capture through the GNOME/Wayland portal

Run the bundled script rather than recreating D-Bus synchronization:

```bash
python3 scripts/portal_screenshot.py --output /absolute/path/to/evidence.png --timeout 20
```

The script keeps one D-Bus connection alive until `org.freedesktop.portal.Request.Response` arrives. This matters because a one-shot `gdbus call` exits before the asynchronous portal response. The portal may show a user confirmation dialog; this is expected security behavior.

Prerequisites: Python 3, `dbus-python`, PyGObject, a running desktop portal, and an interactive graphical session. If any are unavailable, report capture as **blocked** with the failed prerequisite. Never claim visual verification from source code alone.

### 3. Stabilize before capture

After the action that changes the UI, first ensure the target window is foregrounded. The portal captures the desktop, not a requested application; a valid PNG of another foreground window is not evidence about the target. Wait for rendering and loading to settle. Use a bounded delay, normally 1–2 seconds, then capture. For loading indicators or asynchronous assets, take an initial screenshot and a second screenshot after the documented timeout.

### 4. Inspect the image

Use the image-reading capability on the saved absolute path. Check visible headings, selected navigation, loading/error states, clipping, overlap, unexpected selection overlays, and whether the intended application is actually on screen. A successful PNG write proves capture only, not UI correctness.

### 5. Compare against explicit expectations

Record one row per action:

| Action | Expected visible state | Observed visible state | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| tool or interaction | concrete heading/navigation/state | evidence from screenshot | pass/fail/blocked |

Use **pass** only when the screenshot visibly supports the expectation. If the expected application is absent, another window is foregrounded, or the result remains on a default page, use **fail**, not pass.

### 6. Preserve evidence

Store screenshots and a short Markdown report in the project audit directory. Use stable descriptive names such as `01-before.png`, `02-after-action.png`, and `README.md`. Include resolution, capture method, expected-versus-observed results, and any environment limitation.

## Known failure signatures

- `grim: compositor doesn't support the screen capture protocol`: compositor is not exposing wlroots screencopy; switch to the portal.
- GNOME Shell `Screenshot is not allowed`: direct Shell D-Bus API is denied to the caller; switch to the portal.
- One-shot portal call returns only a request object path: the caller exited before the asynchronous response; run the bundled persistent script.
- `import -window root` fails or sees no windows: XWayland tools cannot capture native Wayland surfaces; do not keep retrying X11 tools.
- Synthetic keyboard tools report unsupported virtual keyboard protocol: do not depend on injecting Print Screen; use the portal.

## Verification gate

A desktop verification is complete only when:

1. the screenshot exists and has plausible nonzero dimensions;
2. the image has been inspected, not merely generated;
3. observed content is compared with a stated expectation;
4. failures remain failures in the report;
5. evidence paths are preserved for review.

# Git/NPM Identity

Keep four concerns separate: **project classification**, **Git commit identity**, **GitHub API identity**, and **npm registry credentials**. A matching username alone never proves package access; verify the intended capability against the intended registry.

## Classification

Classify from the canonical absolute project root, not the shell's transient cwd:

- /home/jmercier/Codes/me/** → personal
- /home/jmercier/Codes/Servier/** → Servier professional
- elsewhere → unknown; ask before changing identity or credentials

## Identity matrix

| Context | Git config | GitHub account | npm registry/scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Personal | ~/.gitconfig-personal | bioinfornatics | npmjs, @bioinfornatics/* |
| Servier | ~/.gitconfig-servier | jmservier or approved Servier account | GitHub Packages, @servier/* and @servier-github/* |

Do not assume npm whoami represents the account used by a scoped GitHub Packages request. npm may report the default npmjs identity while scoped package reads use another registry and token.

## Safe diagnostic

Never print tokens. Redact auth lines and report only presence/source.

1. Resolve project and Git roots.
2. Inspect Git identity and remotes.
3. List GitHub accounts with gh auth status and identify the active account.
4. Inspect token scopes from gh auth status; never echo gh auth token.
5. Inspect default and scoped npm registries.
6. Detect whether npm auth is environment-backed, credential-helper-backed, or a literal token in an npmrc.
7. Verify the exact capability with a harmless read operation.

Suggested checks:

```bash
PROJECT_ROOT="$(pwd -P)"
GIT_ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || true)"
git status --short --branch 2>/dev/null || true

```bash
gh auth switch -h github.com -u jmservier
NODE_AUTH_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)" npm view @servier-github/dna version \

A successful npm whoami is optional for package consumption. A successful npm view of the required private package is authoritative.

Typical Servier sequence:

gh auth switch -h github.com -u jmservier
